notes.meaning: Eliphaz steps forward to begin the third and final round of debate with Job. As the oldest and most respected of the three friends, he speaks first each time. Here he gives up gentle reasoning and launches into harsh, direct attacks against Job.

Eliphaz argues that God is completely self-sufficient and gains nothing from human goodness. A person may help himself by living wisely, but our best obedience adds no wealth or happiness to the Creator. While this truth is real, Eliphaz misapplies it by claiming God cares nothing about Job's upright living.

Eliphaz asks with bitter sarcasm if God is punishing Job because Job is so godly. God never brings people into judgment out of fear that they will grow too strong for Him. Therefore, Eliphaz concludes that Job's terrible suffering must be punishment for terrible wrongdoing.

Eliphaz moves from general theories to direct, unfounded accusations against Job. Because Job is suffering so intensely, Eliphaz assumes his sins must be endless and beyond counting. He invents evil deeds to fit his belief that great suffering always equals great sin.

Eliphaz accuses Job of cruel and greedy deeds as a wealthy ruler. He claims Job demanded unfair pledges from poor debtors and stripped them of their only garments for sleeping. He also charges Job with failing in basic hospitality, refusing even a cup of water or a piece of bread to exhausted travellers.

Eliphaz claims that Job used his power to seize land and favoured only the rich and influential. At the same time, he says Job sent poor widows away with nothing and crushed the helpless orphans. None of these charges were true, but Eliphaz stated them as if they were proven facts.

Eliphaz explains that Job's current disaster is the direct punishment for his cruelty to the poor. Traps now surround him, sudden terrors grip his heart, and misery covers him like a rising flood in the dark. In Eliphaz's view, Job is only reaping what he sowed.

Eliphaz points to the high stars to remind Job of how exalted God is above creation. He then falsely accuses Job of believing that God is too far away to notice what happens on earth. He claims Job acted like an atheist who thinks thick clouds hide human wickedness from the eyes of the Lord.

Eliphaz warns Job not to walk the ancient trail followed by rebellious sinners of the past. He points back to the wicked generation before the great flood of Noah, who thought they were safe until sudden destruction washed away their foundations. He warns Job that a similar end awaits anyone who continues down that road.

Eliphaz quotes words Job had used earlier about the ungodly who tell God to leave them alone. Those ancient rebels asked what God could ever do for them, even though He had filled their homes with good things. Eliphaz repeats Job's own words of rejection against Job himself, claiming that he will have nothing to do with such evil thinking.

Eliphaz declares that godly people rejoice when God's justice finally destroys oppressors, like the fire that consumed Sodom. The righteous are glad not out of spite, but because God's holy rule and protection of His people are made clear. He boasts that while Job's possessions were wiped out, he and his friends remain safe under God's favor.

Eliphaz warmly urges Job to make peace with God and stop fighting His discipline. He tells Job to receive instruction from God's mouth and hide His words deep in his heart. The counsel to seek God is excellent in itself, though it wrongly assumes Job was a total stranger to the Lord.

Eliphaz promises that if Job repents and turns back to the Almighty, his ruined life and family will be rebuilt. True repentance must also include throwing out all dishonesty and stolen goods from his tents. Real renewal begins when sin is completely put away.

Job is told to treat his precious gold like common dust and leave his fine treasures among the stones of the dry riverbeds. If he stops trusting in money, the Almighty Himself will become his true treasure and sure defense. Knowing God gives far greater security and joy than piles of silver.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some modern teachers use these verses to promise that turning to God guarantees vast physical riches and financial success, but classic commentators note this reflects Eliphaz's flawed assumption that godliness always brings worldly wealth.

notes.meaning: Eliphaz promises that once Job makes peace with God, fear and gloom will give way to deep joy. Instead of hanging his head in misery and shame, Job will be able to look up toward God with confidence. God will no longer seem like a terrifying enemy, but a beloved Father.

Eliphaz says that when a reconciled person prays, God listens closely and grants his requests. Job will then have joyous reasons to pay the vows and promises he made during his distress. Answered prayers lead naturally to thankful worship.

Eliphaz assures Job that his future plans will succeed because they will align with God's will. Instead of stumbling in the dark as he does now, God's favor and guidance will shine brightly on his path like the morning sun. God brings clarity and blessing to the works of the faithful.

When other people are knocked down by trouble, Job will have the faith to encourage them and say that God lifts people up. God always opposes the proud but rescues those who are humble and broken. Job's restored life would serve as a living testimony of God's saving power.

Eliphaz ends by saying that God will even spare guilty people in answer to the prayers of a clean and righteous man. Without realizing it, Eliphaz speaks words that will come true for himself. At the end of the book, Eliphaz and his friends are forgiven only after God accepts Job's intercession for them.
